Ivy hired a memory erasure clinic to remove every trace of Tobias from her mind. Tobias discovered this only when he visited the local bookshop, finding Ivy treating him as a total stranger while she flirted openly with a young clerk named Peck. Devastated, Tobias went to his friends Nina and Grady, who reluctantly showed him the formal notification letter they had received from the clinic. Furious and heartbroken, Tobias marched straight to the clinic director, Dr. Hallam, demanding to undergo the exact same procedure. Returning to his flat, Tobias painstakingly boxed up every single object connected with Ivy so that the clinic staff could use them to map the specific memories attached to each item.

He remembered the bitter end, when Ivy had come home drunk having dented his car. The ensuing fight was vicious, culminating in her walking out for good. It was the boiling point of months where their relationship had curdled into endless recrimination, driven by her drinking and his cold withholding. 

That night, the clinic technicians Dell and Peck arrived to run the overnight erasure in Tobias's flat. While Tobias lay unconscious, Peck secretly pocketed the boxed mementos, planning to use them to seduce Ivy. Inside his own head, Tobias watched the most recent and ugliest memories of their fights dissolve around him one by one, the shouting faces and slammed doors crumbling into white noise.

The erasure dug deeper, hitting the bedrock of the two years they fell in love. He saw the ice on the frozen river, the steaming bowls at the noodle house, and the glowing screen at the drive-in. Reaching these memories he still loved, Tobias suddenly changed his mind about the procedure. Desperate to save her, he grabbed Ivy's hand in his mind and tried to smuggle her into childhood memories she was never part of, hiding her beneath kitchen tables and in rainstorms from decades past.

Back in the physical world, Dell and the receptionist Rosa got high on Tobias's bed, completely losing track of the procedure as his neural map went off the rails. Panicking, they called Dr. Hallam, who arrived in the middle of the night to re-map the erasure. As he worked, Rosa impulsively kissed him. Hallam's wife caught them and, in a fit of rage, revealed to Rosa that Rosa had previously had her own affair with the doctor, an affair she had willingly chosen to have erased.

Deep in his fading consciousness, Tobias retreated to the last surviving memory, the empty house on the shore where they first connected. As the walls of the house began to collapse into the void, Tobias and Ivy said a tearful goodbye. In the final second before she vanished, she whispered to him to meet her at the beach. That beach was where Tobias and Ivy had first met at a seaside party at the end of the rail line, breaking into that very empty house on the shore to escape the cold.

The erasure completed, and Tobias woke the next morning with no memory that Ivy ever existed. Yet he skipped work on an impulse he could not account for, took the train to the coast, and met Ivy walking aimlessly on the frozen sand. They struck up a conversation, drove back to the city together, and she invited him up to her flat. Meanwhile, a disillusioned Rosa quit the clinic, stole the company records, and mailed the files and session tapes back to every patient on the books. Sitting in Ivy's flat, Tobias and Ivy opened their mail and listened to their own recorded voices tearing each other apart. Horrified by the ugly truths, she ran out into the hallway, but she came back, and looking at each other as strangers with a shared past they could not remember, they agreed to try anyway.

Marcus drove across the city with his partner Rollo, debating foreign drug laws and what fast food was called abroad. They were hitmen on a tight schedule, but as they waited in the corridor outside their target's flat, their argument shifted to whether a foot massage was worth killing a man for. When the time came, Marcus kicked in the door. He recited a passage of scripture with booming authority, and the pair shot a young man named Tobin for double-crossing their employer, Otis. They quickly recovered Otis's stolen briefcase. Suddenly, a fourth man hidden in the bathroom burst out, emptying a revolver at them without hitting either. Standing untouched amidst the bullet holes, Marcus called the survival divine intervention. The realization stayed with him. Later, over breakfast in a coffee shop, two small-time robbers decided on the spot to hold up the diner they were sitting in. When the gunman approached their booth, Marcus remained perfectly calm. He talked the robber down mid-holdup, handed over his own wallet to pacify the man, but kept a firm grip on Otis's briefcase, ultimately letting the couple walk out the door unharmed.

Rollo had never shared his partner's spiritual awakening. Right after surviving the bathroom ambush, Rollo's gun accidentally went off in the back of their moving car, blowing the head off their passenger, Del. Panicked, Marcus parked the bloodied car at his friend Warren's house. A professional fixer arrived, expertly directing the gruesome cleanup and providing the men with fresh clothes. Once presentable, the two hitmen delivered the recovered briefcase to Otis at his bar. While there, they watched Otis paying the ageing boxer Denny to take a dive in the fifth round of an upcoming match. Rollo's evening took a different turn when he bought heroin from his dealer Kip and shot up before a big night out. He had been tasked with taking Otis's wife, Nadia, out for entertainment. They went to a themed diner, dancing well enough to win the evening's dance contest. The night turned disastrous when they returned home. Nadia found Rollo's stash, snorted the heroin mistaking it for cocaine, and instantly overdosed. Rollo frantically drove her to his dealer's house, where she was finally revived by a brutal adrenaline shot straight to the heart on the living-room floor.

Denny's path was shaped by a single heirloom. Years earlier, a returning prisoner of war had delivered to him, then just a young boy, the gold watch his father had kept hidden through years of brutal captivity. That watch meant everything. Now an ageing boxer, Denny decided to double-cross Otis. He ignored the bribe, won the fight, accidentally killed his opponent in the ring, and escaped into the night in a waiting taxi. Hiding out in a cheap motel with his girlfriend Marielle, Denny was horrified to discover she had left his father's watch behind in his flat. Refusing to leave it, Denny returned to his apartment. He found Rollo waiting there and shot the hitman dead with a submachine gun that had been carelessly left on the kitchen counter. Fleeing the scene, Denny crossed paths with Otis. They collided in the street, crashed their vehicles, and stumbled into a pawnshop where the owner took them both prisoner in the basement. Bound and desperate, Denny managed to break free. He was about to escape when he heard Otis's screams. Denny came back downstairs wielding a sword taken from the shop wall and killed the captor who was raping Otis. Covered in blood, Otis declared they were officially square, strictly on the condition that Denny leave town forever. Denny agreed, collected Marielle from the motel, and rode out of the city on a motorcycle taken from the dead pawnshop owner.

The robbery collapsed within a minute, transforming a meticulous plan into absolute chaos. Sirens wailed and glass shattered as Mr. Ash violently shot his way clear of the converging police from the passenger side of the getaway car, the frantic Mr. Elm right beside him. Forced to abandon their compromised vehicle and flee on foot, Mr. Elm desperately hijacked a passing car. The terrified driver panicked, pulled a weapon, and shot him directly in the stomach. Acting on pure adrenaline, a bleeding Mr. Elm shot the driver dead and shoved him aside. Mr. Ash took the wheel, driving the screaming, agonizing Elm to the abandoned warehouse rendezvous. Once inside the cavernous space, Ash dragged him across the concrete, cradled his profusely bleeding body, and swore over and over that he was not going to die.

It was a brutally sharp contrast to the calm morning they had shared just hours before. Over a greasy breakfast, the crew had casually argued about what a popular radio pop song was really about and aggressively debated whether waitresses actually deserved a tip. Shortly after the meal, Bram had handed out the tree aliases for the diamond job, and Mr. Birch had loudly and stubbornly objected to being named Mr. Birch.

For Elm, the journey to that diner table had started much earlier. Undercover officer Danny Roarke had spent grueling hours rehearsing a fabricated anecdote about a tense drug bust in a public toilet with his police handler Pruitt. He practiced every pause and laugh until he could tell it like a genuine, lived memory. Danny had then performed the anecdote perfectly for the crime boss Bram, his volatile son Cal, and the seasoned Mr. Ash, earning their complete trust and being officially taken onto the crew as Mr. Elm. Around that same time, veteran criminal Ren Vasco had walked out of state prison and reported directly to Bram and Cal, who owed him heavily for the years he had loyally kept his mouth shut behind bars.

Back in the bloody, echoing present at the warehouse, the heavy metal doors banged open. Mr. Birch arrived, pacing furiously and covered in sweat. He loudly argued that the job was a deliberate setup with a police informer inside it, and he revealed he had safely hidden the stolen diamonds outside the building. Moments later, Mr. Cedar strolled in with chilling calmness and produced a kidnapped patrolman, Officer Doyle, dragging him from the boot of his car.

When the others briefly stepped away, Mr. Cedar was left entirely alone with the bound and gagged officer. He turned on a radio oldie, danced smoothly to the upbeat rhythm, casually cut off the patrolman's ear with a straight razor, and doused the screaming man in petrol. Before he could strike a match, Mr. Elm raised his weapon and shot Mr. Cedar dead from his bleeding position on the floor. Breathing heavily, Elm told the terrified Doyle that he was a cop and that the police were already waiting outside for Bram to arrive.

Cal returned to the warehouse and found the gruesome scene. He listened to Elm's frantic account of Cedar's madness, then coldly raised his gun and shot Doyle dead himself.

Finally, Bram arrived. He surveyed the carnage and immediately named Mr. Elm as the police informer. Mr. Ash, fiercely loyal to the bleeding man he had saved, absolutely refused to believe the boss and turned his gun directly on Bram. Weapons were drawn in a tense, inescapable triangle. The three-way standoff erupted in a deafening volley of gunfire. When the echoing stopped, Bram, Cal, and Ash had all been shot. Only Ash and Elm were still breathing on the blood-soaked floor.

Coughing violently, Elm looked up at the man who had protected him and confessed that he was indeed a police officer. Pure betrayal washed over Ash's face. He raised his weapon and shot Elm just as the police violently stormed the warehouse, and Ash was instantly cut down by a massive hail of bullets.

On his twenty-fifth birthday, Emmett took control of his vast fortune and summoned the banker Barrow to his office. He told Barrow that of all his sprawling, lucrative holdings, he only wanted to run a failing city newspaper called the Clarion. 

Barrow stared at the young man, his mind slipping back to the miserable day he had acquired him. In a drafty mining boarding house out west, Emmett Rusk's mother had signed her son over to Barrow's guardianship after a defaulted lodger's mine deed unexpectedly made the struggling family rich. The young boy had been furious, driving his wooden sled hard into Barrow's stomach, but he was taken east and away from his parents anyway. 

Now a grown man with boundless capital, Emmett moved his life into the bustling offices of the Clarion. He installed his trusted manager Marsh and his close friend Devlin, and immediately printed a signed statement of principles on the front page. Flush with ambition, Emmett hired away the entire staff of the rival paper, celebrating the coup by throwing a raucous party in the newsroom featuring a brass band and a high-kicking chorus line. 

His personal life moved just as swiftly. Emmett returned from a buying trip abroad engaged to Adele, the governor's niece. However, the romance was short-lived. A run of quiet breakfast-table scenes charted the marriage cooling into bitter silence, the husband and wife sitting miles apart behind separate newspapers. It was around this time that Emmett met the shopgirl Nora Kell on the street, apologizing for the mud splashed on his coat, and soon started visiting her rooms in secret. 

Scandal loomed mid-campaign during Emmett's run for governor. The rival party boss Halloran brought Adele directly to Nora's rooms and threatened total public exposure. Emmett stubbornly refused to withdraw from the race. Consequently, Emmett lost the election, Devlin asked to be transferred to another city to escape the fallout, and the marriage to Adele finally collapsed. 

Free from his first wife, Emmett married Nora and forced her into a lavish opera career for which she had absolutely no voice. Nora's grand debut was a profound public humiliation. A drunk Devlin began drafting a savage review of the performance. Discovering him at the typewriter, Emmett finished the brutal review himself, printed it in the Clarion, and promptly fired Devlin. 

Driven to despair, Nora swallowed poison rather than ever sing again. She survived the attempt, and a shaken Emmett finally let her stop the charade. He shut Nora away in the half-finished, sprawling palace he called Silvermount, where she spent her days working massive jigsaw puzzles in the vast, echoing empty hall. The isolation bred deep resentment. After a joyless beach picnic and a screaming quarrel, Nora packed her bags and left him for good. 

Left entirely alone, Emmett wrecked Nora's bedroom in a violent rage. Amid the torn fabrics and shattered furniture, he found a glass snow globe. He held it up to the light, murmured "Bluebell," and carried it quietly past the endless, reflecting mirrors of his empty mansion. Years later, still alone at Silvermount, Emmett died with the word "Bluebell" on his lips and dropped the snow globe to shatter on the floor. 

A newsreel obituary soon recapped Emmett's towering public life, but it closed without explaining his cryptic last word. The reporter Nash was sent by his editor to find out what "Bluebell" meant. He was quickly turned away by a drunk Nora in a dim seaside nightclub. Undeterred, Nash read Barrow's memoir and interviewed Marsh, Devlin, Nora, and the butler Colm. He ultimately concluded that no single word explains a life, entirely unaware that as he left the estate, workmen were shoveling a childhood sled marked Bluebell into the roaring furnace.

Martin lures Roy to the derelict building, raises his weapon, shoots him in the head, and waits for the flash as he photographs the corpse.

In a motel room he cannot remember checking into, Martin sits on the edge of the bed and narrates the details of an old case down the phone to an anonymous caller.

Corinne hands Martin a vehicle registry record naming Roy Mercer, which she obtained by running a license plate through a friend. This exchange happens shortly after Martin ambushes a man named Vance in a motel bathroom, beats him ruthlessly, and drives him out of town at gunpoint.

Speaking into the motel telephone receiver, Martin explains how, during his career as an insurance investigator, he interviewed a claimant named Elias Prine. Martin firmly ruled the man's profound memory loss to be psychosomatic and officially denied the financial claim.

Corinne hides every pen in her house and deliberately goads Martin into hitting her. She leaves, then returns bruised and blames Vance for the assault so that Martin will blindly go after him. Earlier that day, at her bar, Corinne recognizes the dead man's expensive clothes and the sports car Martin has arrived in. Knowing exactly what he has done, she serves Martin a beer that the staff have spat in.

Martin continues the tragic story of Elias Prine to his unseen caller. Elias's diabetic wife decided to test his condition by asking for insulin injection after injection. She died of the severe overdose he could not remember giving her.

Martin drives to a local tattoo parlor and sits in the artist's chair, having a specific vehicle license plate inked permanently onto his thigh as his vital sixth fact.

Martin details his own tragedy to the voice on the line. Intruders attacked Martin and his wife in their bathroom. Martin killed one of them but was struck violently in the head, permanently losing the ability to form new memories. He explains how he built a strict, reliable system of instant photographs, annotated notes, and body tattoos to hunt the second attacker, a man he knows only by the initials R.M.

Rather than believe a devastating revelation, Martin deliberately burns his instant photographs of a dead man. He writes the warning that he is lying to you on his Polaroid picture of Roy, and copies down Roy's license plate as his next target. This frantic cover-up occurs right after Roy arrives and tells Martin that the man he just killed was entirely innocent, that Martin already avenged his wife a year ago, and that Martin is himself the man in the Elias Prine story.

About a year before the main action, a plainclothes officer called Roy actually helps Martin find and kill the real attacker, a killing Martin forgets within minutes. Unaware of his completed vengeance, Martin later gathers and burns his wife's hairbrush and books in an empty field, trying desperately to grieve a loss he can never retain.

Martin changes into a dead man's tailored suit and takes the keys to his sports car. He does this because, as the man died, he whispered the name Elias, a reference which Martin cannot explain. Moments before this, Martin fiercely beats and strangles the drug dealer Gil in a derelict basement and photographs the bloody body.

The anonymous caller finally feeds Martin a name and a location over the motel phone, identifying the drug dealer Gil Marsh as the man he is looking for.

Aaron admits to Lena that he is carrying her husband's heart in his chest. She screams and throws him out of the house into the cold street. She opens the door and takes him back into her home. Aaron purchases a heavy black handgun and tracks Wes to a roadside motel. Lena demands that Wes be killed for what he has done. Aaron packs his bags and leaves his estranged wife Della. He speaks to Della plainly, telling her he does not want the child she is trying to conceive.

Mathematician Aaron Vale sits in a sterile clinic and hears a doctor say his failing heart will kill him within weeks unless a donor is found. Wes follows Aaron and Lena back to their own rented motel room. Wes stands in the doorway and asks Aaron to finish the job. Aaron raises the weapon and turns the gun on himself instead. Lena Ward is a recovered addict living a perfectly settled suburban life. She shares a quiet home with her husband Doug and their two young daughters.

The heavy grille of Wes's pickup hits Doug and both girls at a pedestrian crossing. He drives off down the avenue. He turns the truck back toward the intersection. He flees the scene entirely. Della presses Aaron to agree to be inseminated with his frozen sperm before his condition claims his life. Lena and Wes carry the dying Aaron into an emergency room. The transplanted heart in Aaron's chest fails completely. Wes walks away and goes home to his family. Lena, carrying a child, goes home alone to an empty house.

Aaron holds the gun but cannot go through with the execution. He pulls the trigger and only wounds Wes in the shoulder. He lowers the weapon and tells Wes to run away. Lena goes back to using cocaine. She sits in dark rooms and begins methodically destroying herself with the drug. Ex-convict Wes Tarrow is a newly born again believer. He holds down a steady job and coaches boys' baseball on the weekends. His wife Nita watches him quietly, dreading his intense fanaticism and his unpredictable temper.

Doug's heart is transplanted into Aaron's failing body. Aaron opens his eyes and wakes up feeling alive for the first time in months. Wes walks through the double doors of a local police station. He confesses to the hit-and-run and is sent back to a state prison. Aaron follows Lena through the city streets. He engineers a casual meeting at a public swimming pool. Aaron and Lena begin an intense romantic affair.

Released early from his sentence, Wes packs a single bag and walks out on Nita and on his religious faith. He takes up menial work at a motel located far from his home. Lena sits in a bright waiting area and is told at the hospital that her husband and both of her children are dead. Aaron lies awake, unable to stop thinking about whose heart is beating inside his chest. He hires a private investigator to locate the donor's widow.

An immigrant shopkeeper named Nadir and his young daughter Sahar stood at the counter of a sporting goods store, purchasing a handgun while the dealer openly mocked Nadir’s heavy accent. Across town, the night was already unraveling. Trey and Kwame waited in the shadows outside an upscale restaurant, ambushing the city prosecutor, Halstead, and violently carjacking his luxury sedan. 

Days from now, Detective Isaiah Reece would be called to a desolate roadside to examine a dumped, burned body, only to look down and realize the charred remains belonged to his brother, Kwame. Standing in the morgue later that same week, Reece’s grieving mother would strike him, bitterly blaming the detective for never once going to look for his brother when he had the chance. 

But tonight, Kwame was still alive, speeding away in a stolen car, while the city’s fractures deepened elsewhere. Officer Boyle pulled over a wealthy black couple, Clay and Renee Hobart. Under the guise of a routine search, Boyle maliciously groped Renee right in front of her husband before letting them go with a mocking warning. Disgusted by the display, Boyle’s partner, Voss, marched into their commander’s office at the end of the shift, demanding a new patrol car rather than spend another minute riding with a racist. 

The next morning, a locksmith named Mateo arrived to change the locks at the Halstead residence. Paula Halstead hovered nearby, loudly and baselessly assuming the tattooed man was a gang member who was going to sell copies of her keys to his friends. Shrugging off the insult, Mateo moved on to his next job at Nadir’s shop. He replaced the lock but warned the shopkeeper that the door frame itself was completely broken. Frustrated and paranoid, Nadir accused Mateo of running a con to extort more money. 

By the end of the week, this misunderstanding would culminate in violence. Nadir would wait in the shadows outside Mateo’s house, raising his newly purchased handgun and firing a shot just as Mateo’s small daughter, Rosie, ran joyfully into her father’s arms. 

Before that fateful shot could be fired, the city continued its grind. Officer Boyle sat in a sterile office, pleading with a health insurance clerk named Delia Frank to approve an experimental treatment for his dying father, only to be coldly refused. Overnight, Nadir’s shop was entirely smashed and looted. When he filed a claim, his insurer refused to pay a dime because he had ignored the locksmith’s explicit warning about the faulty door. 

The roads grew treacherous. Renee Hobart found herself trapped upside down in a burning vehicle after a horrific wreck. It was Boyle, the very officer who had assaulted her days prior, who crawled into the flaming wreckage and dragged her to safety. Elsewhere on the streets, Trey and Kwame recklessly ran down a shopkeeper named Pham. Panicking, they loaded the bleeding man into their vehicle and dumped him unceremoniously outside a hospital emergency room. 

The chaos bled into the wealthy suburbs. Clay Hobart, pushed to the brink by his own helplessness, was stopped mid-carjacking of his very own vehicle. A swarm of police drew their weapons, but Voss stepped in, talking the other officers out of shooting the distraught man. Shortly after, Clay found himself behind the wheel, driving Trey away from a police pursuit at breakneck speed before angrily throwing the young criminal out of the moving car. 

Outside Mateo’s house, the gunshot echoed through the neighborhood. But the child remained untouched. Sahar, fearing her father’s rage, had bought blanks instead of live ammunition. Dropping the gun, Nadir fell to his knees, deciding in a tearful instant that the unharmed little girl was his guardian angel. 

Meanwhile, Voss drove down a dark highway and picked up Kwame, who was hitchhiking after losing his ride. When Kwame nervously reached into his pocket, Voss misread the movement, drew his service weapon, and shot the young man dead, subsequently burning the car and the body on the roadside. 

In her sprawling, empty home, Paula Halstead took a terrible tumble down her staircase. Lying bruised on the floor, she looked up at her housekeeper, Alba, and tearfully confessed that the woman she paid to clean was the only real friend she had. Across the city, Trey stumbled upon Pham’s abandoned van. Opening the back, he found it packed with terrified, trafficked migrants. Instead of selling them to a new syndicate, Trey drove to the docks and turned them loose into the freezing night. 

As the first snow of the year began to fall, tires slipped on the icy pavement. Another collision occurred at a busy intersection, and immediately, another angry argument echoed into the winter street.

Ruben shared a cramped house with his mother, his violent brother Nestor, Nestor's wife Alma, and their baby. Nestor spent his nights robbing pharmacies and beating Alma, prompting Ruben to desperately press her to run away with him. Looking for a way out, Ruben discovered that Nestor's rottweiler, Tigre, killed other dogs on sight. He started entering the beast in local dogfights, winning steadily and hoarding the cash. Hoping to force an end, Ruben paid two thugs to beat Nestor. Instead of submitting, Nestor responded by taking Alma, the baby, and Ruben's hidden savings, disappearing completely. Desperate to rebuild his funds, Ruben arranged one last fight, but the promoter, Chaco, pulled a gun and shot Tigre in the ring. Enraged, Ruben stabbed Chaco and fled with his friend Pipo, hauling the bleeding dog into their vehicle. Speeding blindly through the city streets, Ruben ran a red light at speed and ploughed violently into another car. Much later, after Nestor was shot dead robbing a bank, Ruben attended the funeral, only for Alma to coldly refuse his final offer to leave with him.

Before the crash at the intersection, model Celine Vaz had been living a charmed life. Her lover, Hector, had walked out on his wife and daughters to move Celine into a luxurious new flat that directly faced her own towering billboard. That glamorous life shattered when Ruben's speeding car struck hers. Celine woke in the hospital with her shattered leg pinned together, frantic because her beloved lapdog, Chispa, was lost somewhere in the cavernous new flat. While she lay trapped in a sterile bed, Chispa fell through a hole in the floorboards. Hector spent days frantically tearing up the floor trying to reach the trapped animal, neglecting Celine as her pinned leg turned gangrenous. Ultimately, Celine's leg had to be amputated, and as she grieved her lost limb, the city outside her window took down the billboard carrying her perfect, whole image.

Cardo, a former guerrilla turned vagrant contract killer, happened to be standing at the junction when Ruben's car slammed into Celine's. Ignoring the human wreckage, Cardo dragged the bleeding rottweiler, Tigre, out of the crushed vehicle. He took the beast home and nursed him back to health among his own pack of strays. Soon after, a wealthy businessman named Elian hired Cardo to murder his half-brother and business partner, Sergio. Cardo’s mind, however, was on his own fractured family. He watched from a distance as his estranged wife was buried, then quietly followed his grown daughter, Perla, to her home. Returning to his yard, Cardo found that Tigre had killed every other dog in his pack while he was out. Cardo put a gun to the rottweiler’s head, but staring into the animal's eyes, he found he could not fire. Instead of executing his contract, Cardo abducted Sergio and chained him up in his squalid lair instead of killing him. He then brought Elian face to face with his captive brother, left a loaded pistol on the table between them, and walked out, having calmly taken money from both men. Cardo broke into Perla's flat while she was out. He left a long, recorded confession of who he really was on her answering machine and took a single photograph of her. Shaved and dressed in clean clothes, Cardo left all his accumulated money on Perla's counter. With nothing left to tie him to the city, he walked out into the desolate wasteland with Tigre at his side.

In a flat overlooking the neon-lit street, an old man stood by the window. He gestured toward the flashing sirens below, explaining in a quiet, gravelly voice to the younger man beside him that absolutely nothing survives time, not even the fiercest of passions or the most violent of nights.

Down on that very street, the flashing sirens belonged to waiting police cruisers. Officers aggressively handcuffed Cort and Jonah, their clothes stained with dark blood, and carried the struggling pair out of the heavy doors of a nightclub and into the cool night air. 

Inside the club, the air had just been thick with screaming. Jonah stood over a broken figure, methodically beating the man's face in with a heavy red fire extinguisher. Only a few feet away, hidden in the shifting shadows of the strobe lights, the real Adder stood perfectly still, watching the brutal mistake unfold with cold amusement.

Moments before the extinguisher was lifted, Cort was hunting frantically through the packed, pulsing dance floor of the club. Desperate and enraged, he lunged and seized the man he thought was the culprit, only for the stranger's companions to swarm him, twisting Cort's limb until his arm snapped with a sickening crack.

The furious momentum that carried them into the club had begun just outside on the pavement. Two shadowy men lingering in the street had approached the frantic pair, offering to sell Cort the rapist's name for a fistful of cash. Taking the money, they steered Cort and Jonah toward the thumping bass of the club known as the Pit.

They had been desperately searching the streets because of what they found outside the house. Cort and Jonah had stumbled out of the loud, crowded party, laughing and shouting, only to freeze in horror. There, illuminated by harsh rotating lights, they found Lise being loaded onto a stretcher and lifted into the back of a waiting ambulance.

She was bleeding profusely from her skull. In the damp dark of a concrete tunnel, the Adder had raped Lise, mercilessly beating her head against the hard wall. A lone passer-by had paused at the tunnel's edge, glimpsed the violent struggle, and silently backed away into the night without saying a word.

Lise had only been in the tunnel to avoid the traffic. Rather than cross the busy, dangerous road above, she had descended into the pedestrian underpass. As she rounded the corner, she walked straight in on a pimp known as the Adder, who was viciously beating a transsexual woman against the damp tiles.

She was walking alone because she had reached her limit. At the party, Cort had gotten steadily drunk and high, his behavior becoming increasingly erratic as he started aggressively pursuing other women. Disgusted and exhausted by his antics, Lise had turned on her heel and left the house on her own.

The mood had been so different on the way there. Lise, Cort, and Jonah had ridden the underground together to reach the party, the carriage echoing with their laughter as they cheerfully argued about sex, boundaries, and Cort's legendary, reckless drinking habits.

Earlier that afternoon, the world had felt peaceful. Lise sat on a wooden bench, reading quietly in a sunlit park. Sprinklers ticked back and forth over the green grass, and children played loudly in the distance. She smiled, one hand resting gently, protectively, on her flat stomach.

The instinct to guard her stomach was brand new. Alone in the quiet bathroom of her flat, Lise had nervously taken a pregnancy test. She stared at the plastic wand, her breath catching in her throat when she saw the unmistakable lines indicating that it was positive.

The morning had begun with such simple intimacy. Lise was lying in bed, tangled in the sheets with Cort. She was softly describing a recurring dream she kept having about a long, pulsing red tunnel. Cort listened, smiling, and soon the heavy atmosphere broke as the two began playfully teasing each other about her lingering ex-boyfriend, Jonah.

I hadn't slept in weeks. As a product recall investigator, my life was a blur of hotel rooms and flight cabins. The only thing that finally let me close my eyes was weeping into the shoulders of strangers at support groups for terminal diseases I did not have. It was a pathetic, peaceful existence. But peace is fragile. Months from now, this will all end with me bleeding in a high-rise stairwell, putting a gun in my own mouth to kill a man who does not exist, before holding a woman's hand at a window as the city's debt-record towers detonate and crumble to the ground.

That is exactly how far this will go. But before the explosives, before the gun, there was Ada Vey. Ada started attending the same support groups, and her obvious faking destroyed my emotional release. With my insomnia back in full force, I stumbled through my days. On a routine business flight, I met a soap salesman named Rex Marrow. He was everything I was not, and I pocketed his business card before we parted ways.

Soon after, my flat and every piece of my carefully curated catalogue furniture were destroyed in a sudden explosion. With nowhere else to go, I called Rex. He took me in, moving me into a rotting, derelict house at the absolute edge of the industrial district. That night, outside a local bar, Rex asked me to do him a favor and hit him as hard as I could. I swung, and the two of us proceeded to beat each other bloody in the car park.

What started as two men brawling in the dark hardened into a weekly basement club. It had its own strict rules and quickly began pulling in more and more members who needed the same visceral release. Meanwhile, Ada resurfaced. She overdosed, and Rex brought her back to the derelict house to recover. Almost immediately, the two of them began a loud, violent affair that echoed through the thin walls, an arrangement I absolutely could not stand.

Rex was enterprising. He began rendering human fat, stolen from the dumpsters of a high-end cosmetic surgery clinic, into premium soap. He sold it right back to the luxury department stores at eighty dollars a bar. His lessons grew harsher. One night, Rex poured lye onto my wet hand, burning the skin, and physically held me there, absolutely refusing to let me retreat into my guided meditation. He wanted me to hit bottom. I took that energy to work, blackmailing my employer into paying me a full salary simply to stay away, using my heavily beaten face as the undeniable evidence of my instability.

Rex took the money and the momentum, turning our basement club into a militant organization he called Havoc. He filled the derelict house with shaven recruits who mindlessly took his orders and ventured out to vandalize corporate property. The chaos escalated until Rex deliberately steered our car into oncoming traffic, letting the vehicle roll and crash. When the dust settled, Rex had completely disappeared.

Through the long, heavy night, helicopters passed over every neighbourhood in the city, spraying a thick mist to eradicate crop pests. Beneath the thrumming rotors, Doctor Neil Hartigan and his wife Bess, a painter, stood in their bedroom getting ready for a dinner party. Across town, the baker Otto Kemp wiped down his counter and took a phone order for a large birthday cake for a boy called Charlie Rill.

The next morning, Charlie was knocked down by a car driven by a waitress called Rhona on his way to school. He picked himself up, dusted off his knees, and walked home, insisting to everyone that he was perfectly fine. Hours later, Charlie collapsed into a deep coma. His frantic parents, Grant and Elaine, rushed him to the ward and began to keep a ceaseless vigil at the hospital. The sterile silence of the waiting room was broken when Grant's estranged father, Duff, turned up out of the blue. Sitting rigidly on a plastic chair, Duff confessed to an affair he had hidden for decades. Meanwhile, unpaid for the lavish birthday cake and feeling entirely ignored, the baker Otto started making anonymous, menacing phone calls to the Rill family's empty house.

In another corner of the city, telephone-sex worker Cheryl sat in her living room, calmly talking men through their darkest fantasies. Beside her on the sofa, her husband Stu seethed in silent, mounting rage. Needing an escape, Stu and three friends drove out to the country to fish, only to find a young woman's body floating face down in the river. Rather than call the authorities, the men simply tethered the body to the muddy bank and carried on fishing for two more days before finally telling anyone. When they returned, Vern's wife Iris, who worked as a party clown, was utterly disgusted when she learned what the men had done, her painted smile giving way to a horrified grimace.

Downtown, the singer Vida performed nightly in a smoky club, basking in the spotlight, while her cellist daughter Bee sat alone at home, drawing solemn, solitary notes from her strings. Not far away, Officer Rowe was busy cheating on his wife Peg with a woman called Nan. Tangled in his own deceit, Rowe callously abandoned the family dog on a distant roadside just to cover one of his elaborate lies. But Nan's own life was unravelling; her ex-husband Cass, a helicopter pilot, learned she had a new man and flew into a jealous rage, breaking into her home and sawing her furniture to pieces.

While Neil and Bess Hartigan were away at their dinner party, Ike and Dot house-sat for them. Bored and restless, they spent the evening photographing Dot vividly made up to look like a beaten corpse. At the dinner party itself, the wine flowed too freely, and Bess suddenly admitted to a long-ago nude modelling session and a secret affair. Neil shattered the sophisticated atmosphere, making a furious, shouting scene in front of their hosts. 

At the hospital, Charlie Rill finally died. Shattered by grief, Grant and Elaine left the ward and went directly to the bakery to confront Otto about his cruel phone calls. Instead of a fight, the baker broke down, fed the starving parents warm bread, and grieved bitterly with them in the flour-dusted kitchen. 

That same night, Bee found her mother Vida asleep after her gig. The young cellist walked into the garage, closed the door tight, and killed herself with the car engine running. 

The next afternoon, at a sunlit picnic in the hills, Stu's simmering rage boiled over, and he smashed a young woman's head with a heavy rock. 

Shortly after, a deep, violent tremor shook the entire city to its foundations. When the dust settled, every death, every shattered secret, and every quiet wreck was folded seamlessly into one brief evening bulletin.

Emlyn stood in the center of the living room, his expression perfectly placid. He explained that he had known the truth for four years, ever since his wife had told him during their trip abroad. With a faint smirk, he added that he had never thought much of his friend’s letters, either.

This confrontation had been inevitable from the moment Wilder had picked up the telephone earlier that same evening. Panicked and in a frantic state, the book agent had rung Emlyn, demanding he come over to the house immediately. 

The panic had set in just moments before the phone call, when Odile had casually let slip a piece of professional betrayal. She mentioned that Emlyn had been quietly publishing a certain writer—a man whom Wilder represented, and whom both Wilder and Emlyn mutually, intensely detested. 

The revelation of this spiteful business deal occurred in a dim, quiet bar, two years after the affair had ended. Odile sat across from Wilder, nursing her drink, and told him that her marriage was officially over. She claimed that she had spent the entirety of the previous night confessing everything to her husband. 

The affair itself had concluded with far less drama. Eventually, Wilder and Odile had simply decided that maintaining the rented rooms had become a tedious chore. They methodically split the crockery between them, packed up their belongings, and surrendered the lease. 

Before the spark completely died, there had been a suffocating dinner at the married couple’s house. Over the meal, the two men engaged in an endless, animated discussion about racquet games and schoolboy sports. They carried on with such intense camaraderie that Odile was left with no part in the talk at all, sitting in silence at her own table.

That dinner had followed a long, boozy restaurant lunch between the two men. Emlyn drank heavily through the afternoon with Wilder, relentlessly baiting the agent about the state of contemporary fiction, yet never once mentioning a word about what he had learned of the betrayal.

He had kept his silence even when Odile first returned from their trip. She had gone straight back to the rented rooms to meet Wilder, saying nothing whatever about the vacation or what had transpired. The afternoon passed exactly as all the others had, wrapped in their usual secrecy.

The secret, however, had already been laid bare. In a hotel room abroad, Odile had finally confessed the affair to her husband. Emlyn had absorbed the blow, merely remarking with a cold detachment that he had always been fonder of his friend than of his wife.

The confession was forced by Emlyn’s sharp eye. Earlier in the trip, he had approached the hotel desk and asked his wife about a letter being held for her—a letter addressed in a neat, familiar hand he instantly recognized as Wilder’s.

Before the trip, the clandestine relationship had faced its first true complication. Odile had arrived at their secret sanctuary and announced that she was carrying her husband’s child. Despite the heavy news, the pair had decided that their time in the rented rooms would go on exactly as before.

Those rooms had been their private world. Wilder and Odile had rented them in a quiet, unassuming district, filling the spaces with fresh linen and matching plates, giving the illicit affair a domestic household of its very own. 

It had all begun in a stolen moment of opportunity. During a lively party at the house of his closest friend, Wilder had discreetly led Odile away from the noise, guiding her to an upstairs room. There, while the other guests drank and laughed downstairs, the book agent leaned in close and told her just how lovely she was.

The extraterrestrials explain patiently that every moment exists at once, suspended in a permanent state, and that free will is a bizarre, localized idea peculiar only to his own planet. They observe all of existence as a single, unchanging landscape of events.

A great city is destroyed by fire in a single night, reduced to a vast expanse of smoking ash and fused rubble. The prisoners, who have been waiting out the inferno down in a subterranean meat locker, come up to the surface to find the entire metropolis completely gone.

He marries the daughter of a man who owns a lucrative optometry school. Through this union and the business connections it provides, he becomes an exceptionally rich man, surrounded by the comforts of a highly successful practice.

He is lost behind the lines in a bleak, freezing landscape, accompanied by a hostile scout. The scout beats him harshly because he simply wants to be left alone in the cold wilderness to die in peace.

He is shot dead by an invisible beam weapon immediately after addressing a large crowd from a podium. This execution happens exactly as he has always known it would, an unavoidable fact of his existence.

His father throws him directly into the deep end of a public swimming pool to teach him how to swim through sudden immersion. He sinks like a stone to the very bottom of the tiled basin.

He is sent on to a great city as a captive. Upon arrival, he is housed with a large group of other prisoners in a massive, disused abattoir, surrounded by the lingering atmosphere of the slaughterhouse.

He goes on a local radio talk show, leaning into the microphone to try to tell the world the absolute truth about the aliens and the mechanics of the fourth dimension.

The pair are captured by enemy forces. The scout suffers from a severe infection and dies of gangrene on the crowded prison train, using his last ragged breath to blame him for the grim fate that has befallen them.

He comes home, suffers a sudden collapse, and is hospitalized in a quiet ward. There, another patient introduces him to the erratic, imaginative works of a hack science fiction writer.

He is taken by extraterrestrial beings and transported across the void. He is kept in a transparent zoo enclosure on their distant planet, sharing the habitat with a kidnapped film actress for the amusement of alien spectators.

The prisoners are made to dig countless bodies out of the ruined cellars. The gruesome labor continues without pause until one of the diggers collapses and dies of the dry heaves.

A boy is born in a small, smoke-stained industrial town. He exists as a remarkably weak and peculiar child, entirely out of step with his surroundings.

He survives a horrific air crash in the jagged peaks of a mountain range. His wife dies of carbon monoxide poisoning from a faulty exhaust pipe while frantically driving her car to the hospital to see him.

A fellow prisoner makes a solemn, unbending promise to have him killed one day, swearing vengeance purely on the dead scout's account.

He is held in a sprawling prison camp situated directly beside a compound of enemy officers. These officers have been drawing double rations for years due to an unnoticed clerical error, living in relative luxury.

His daughter decides firmly that he is senile. Acting on this conviction, she legally takes all of his business and personal affairs completely out of his hands.

He is conscripted into the military to serve as a chaplain's assistant. He is shipped overseas to a zone of conflict with absolutely no training worth the name, entirely unprepared for the reality of the situation.

Dressed in the heavy robes of devout pilgrims, Solly Two Coats and his crew walked calmly into a diamond house in a northern port and walked out carrying a massive, flawless stone. Word of the daring heist traveled fast. Overseas, his cousin Marv caught wind of the score and immediately ordered Solly to bring the diamond straight over to him. 

Before leaving, Solly crossed paths with Grigor the Nail. Grigor casually mentioned a prime bookmaker's operating in the city. At the exact same time, Grigor secretly tipped off two pawnbrokers, Ike and Benno, telling them to ambush and rob Solly when he arrived at the betting shop. 

Meanwhile, boxing promoters Halloway and Digby sent their fighter, Pretty Sam, to a local camp of travellers to purchase a caravan. The negotiation went sour quickly. A bare-knuckle fighter named Finn took offense to the deal and knocked Sam out cold. This left Halloway in a desperate bind, as he suddenly had no man to put up in the ruthless gang boss Coldstone's upcoming fixed bout. With no other options, Halloway was forced to put the unpredictable Finn in the fight instead. He swore to a very dangerous Coldstone that Finn would absolutely take a dive and go down in the fourth round.

Solly finally landed in the city. He promptly delivered the massive diamond to a fence named Hersch, then headed straight for the bookmaker's Grigor had recommended to place a bet on the upcoming fight. Waiting in the shadows were Ike, Benno, and their accomplice Tulley. They lunged at Solly, bungling the robbery in their panic. They took hold of Solly's arm and his locked case, but before they could secure their prize, Grigor suddenly appeared and chased the pawnbrokers off. 

That night at the boxing match, Finn ignored his instructions entirely. He unleashed a brutal hook and knocked his opponent out cold in the very first round. Coldstone lost an absolute fortune on the bets and immediately took his furious vengeance out on Halloway. 

Across town, Marv flew into the city expecting his diamond. Finding Solly completely missing, Marv hired the lethal bounty hunter Ledge to track him down. Grigor, however, had already taken Solly captive. Desperate for the loot, Grigor callously cut off Solly's arm just to get the locked case open, only to find that the massive stone was not inside it. 

Ledge's hunt yielded quick results. He traced the pawnbrokers, ambushed them, and shot their car to pieces, taking both the terrified pawnbrokers and the diamond they had somehow acquired. Elsewhere, Coldstone acquired the mutilated Solly and brutally fed him to his pigs. The gang boss then summoned Halloway and Digby, explicitly detailing the gruesome fate that awaited them if the second arranged fight went wrong. 

Terrified, Halloway and Digby cornered Finn and explicitly told him he had to go down in the fourth round. To ensure compliance, Coldstone's men visited the traveller camp and mercilessly burned Finn's mother to death inside her caravan. 

Bloodshed continued to spill into the streets. Grigor managed to ambush Ledge's car while Ike and Benno were still trapped inside. A chaotic shootout erupted, leaving Ledge, Grigor, and Benno dead on the asphalt. In the confusion, Tulley managed to slip away, taking with him a dog that had accidentally swallowed the massive diamond during the chaos. 

The night of the second fight arrived. Driven by pure grief and rage, Finn stepped into the ring and knocked his opponent out once again in the fourth round. As the body hit the mat, the travellers unleashed their vengeance, massacring Coldstone's men directly in the roaring crowd. Amidst the slaughter, Halloway and Digby tracked down Coldstone and shot him dead. By the time morning broke, the travellers had completely vanished. 

Days later, the wandering dog was handed in at a quiet local pet shop. The animal promptly coughed up the massive diamond right onto the floor, and through a bizarre twist of fate, Halloway and Digby ended up holding it.
